strengths: Practical and well-motivated system perspective: The paper directly tackles the critical gap between algorithmic cooperative perception and edge deployability by addressing both model compute latency and communication bandwidth simultaneously.

Comprehensive full-stack design: Rather than isolating PTQ or feature compression, the work integrates a codebook-based communication compression strategy with full-pipeline PTQ (covering encoder, fusion, and head) calibrated specifically for multi-agent settings.

Domain-specific PTQ calibration: The proposed alignment module introduces multi-agent sampling, a heterogeneity alignment loss (KL divergence on fused BEV features), and a spatial alignment loss on box outputs to handle multi-sensor and cross-agent misalignment under quantization noise.

Extensive hardware and deployment evaluation: The authors conduct thorough latency breakdown measurements on physical hardware (TensorRT with custom CUDA kernels and ROS), reporting power/energy consumption (QPS/W) and evaluating realistic communication delays on multiple datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, and OPV2V).
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental: The communication compression relies heavily on codebook representations similar to CodeFilling (Hu et al., CVPR 2024), and the base PTQ pipeline heavily builds upon established techniques like AdaRound and BRECQ/LiDAR-PTQ. The primary algorithmic novelty is confined to the auxiliary alignment losses during calibration.

Mathematical typo in communication bandwidth formulas: In Section 2.3.1, the bandwidth formulas are written with an outer logarithm: $\log_2 (H \times W \times C \times 32 / 8)$ and $\log_2 (H \times W \times \log_2(n_L) \times n_R / 8)$. The data volume in bytes should simply be $H \times W \times C \times 4$ (or bits $32 H W C$); wrapping the entire size in $\log_2$ is mathematically incorrect.

Severe degradation on Transformer architectures: As shown in Table 1, attention-based fusion (V2X-ViT) drops precipitously under INT4/8 quantization (from 57.4/49.5 AP30/50 down to 29.9/8.8), showing that the proposed calibration strategy still struggles significantly with attention mechanisms and LayerNorm operations.

Mixed results in component ablation: In Table 2 (DAIR-V2X LP + LS), adding the spatial alignment loss $\mathcal{L}_{spatial}$ slightly decreases performance compared to adding only $\mathcal{L}_{hetero}$ (80.8/75.3 down to 80.2/75.5), yet no discussion is provided regarding the interplay or balancing weights between these losses.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical bottleneck in V2X cooperative perception, where existing methods often ignore the intertwined hardware computation, edge memory constraints, and network communication latency.

The full-stack perspective—combining model quantization (PTQ across encoder, fusion, and head) with communication message quantization via codebooks—provides a holistic and well-motivated system design.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V) and multiple intermediate fusion paradigms (CNN, attention, pooling-based), demonstrating strong accuracy preservation down to INT4 weight / INT8 activation for CNN architectures.

System-level latency profiling on TensorRT with custom CUDA kernels and realistic transmission delay modeling provides credible evidence of real-world deployability and speedups (3.2x end-to-end latency reduction).
weaknesses: The core algorithmic contributions are somewhat incremental: codebook-based feature compression heavily draws upon existing techniques (e.g., CodeFilling), and the calibration pipeline largely adapts existing PTQ techniques (e.g., AdaRound, Min-max calibration) with auxiliary distillation losses ($L_{hetero}$ and $L_{spatial}$).

Notational and mathematical imprecisions in Section 2: in Section 2.3.1, the transmission bandwidth formulas mistakenly wrap the byte count in $\log_2(\cdot)$ (e.g., $\log_2(H \times W \times C \times 32 / 8)$ instead of the raw data volume). Furthermore, in Algorithm 1, the interplay between the discrete scale factor search (Eq. 8) and parameter optimization via gradient minimization of $L_{hetero}$ and $L_{spatial}$ (lines 11 and 16) is somewhat vague and should be detailed more rigorously.

Limited effectiveness on vision transformer backbones: as shown in Table 1, the approach experiences severe degradation on attention-heavy architectures like V2X-ViT (dropping from 57.4% to 29.9% AP30 under INT4/INT8), highlighting that the proposed calibration and alignment scheme struggles with transformer-based multi-agent fusion.

Evaluation hardware mismatch with edge motivation: while the paper is motivated by resource-constrained in-vehicle edge platforms, hardware measurements and power benchmarks are conducted on a desktop NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU (consuming ~300W), rather than typical automotive embedded hardware (e.g., NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin/Drive Orin).

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: While most cooperative perception research focuses on accuracy under idealized full-precision assumptions, this paper tackles the real-world deployment bottlenecks of inference compute, communication bandwidth, and system latency simultaneously.

Comprehensive full-stack perspective: Unifies model-level quantization (weights and activations) with communication-level quantization (codebook-indexed BEV feature sharing), providing a holistic system-level treatment of end-to-end V2X perception delay.

Well-motivated alignment objectives: The introduction of heterogeneity alignment loss (KL divergence) and spatial alignment loss (bounding-box regression consistency) appropriately addresses key domain-specific challenges in V2X, such as multi-modal sensor discrepancies and spatial/pose noise.

Extensive experimental evaluation: Validated across multiple datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V) and multiple fusion backbones (Pyramid Fusion, AttFuse, Where2comm, etc.), complemented by deployment latency breakdowns (TensorRT profiling) and energy efficiency measurements.
weaknesses: Ambiguity between Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) and full retraining: While Section 2.4 frames the model compression as lightweight PTQ requiring minimal data, Section 2.3.2 describes a codebook learning stage where all model parameters (encoder, fusion module, detection head) are unfrozen and jointly fine-tuned on task and reconstruction losses. This means the overall pipeline is not strictly post-training/training-free, and the computational cost of the codebook adaptation stage should be clarified.

Evaluation on non-embedded hardware: System latency, throughput, and power consumption are measured on a desktop GPU (NVIDIA RTX 3090). While informative, real V2X deployments operate on automotive edge compute platforms (e.g., NVIDIA Jetson Orin/Xavier or automotive-grade ECUs), where memory bandwidth constraints and INT8/INT4 Tensor Core behaviors differ notably.

Moderate algorithmic novelty: Several individual components rely heavily on established techniques (e.g., vector quantization/codebooks from CodeFilling, AdaRound, and standard PTQ calibration). The primary contribution lies in system synthesis and the specific calibration loss formulation rather than a fundamentally new quantization algorithm.

Sensitivity on Transformer-based architectures: Table 1 reveals that attention-heavy architectures like V2X-ViT suffer severe performance degradation under INT4/INT8 (AP30 dropping from 57.4 to 29.9), indicating that the current calibration and alignment strategies are less effective for transformer-based cross-agent attention.

strengths: Compelling and practically motivated focus: The paper tackles a critical and often overlooked bottleneck in V2X cooperative perception—the high computational, memory, and communication overhead of full-precision intermediate fusion models on resource-constrained vehicular platforms.

Holistic full-stack system design: QuantV2X effectively integrates communication-side compression (codebook index transmission) and model-side compression (end-to-end post-training quantization across encoders, fusion modules, and detection decoders).

Realistic, deployment-centric evaluation: Instead of relying solely on static offline accuracy, the work evaluates system-level latency (local inference, transmission, and fusion inference) on TensorRT/ROS and demonstrates how latency reduction translates into substantial downstream performance gains in dynamic online settings (e.g., +9.5 mAP30 on V2X-Real and real-world evaluation in V2X-ReaLO).

Domain-specific quantization design: Proposes tailored alignment mechanisms—such as the multi-agent calibration sampling strategy, heterogeneity alignment loss, and spatial alignment loss—that directly address cross-agent modality shifts and pose/spatial noise under low-bit quantization.

Extensive experimental validation: The empirical evaluation spans multiple datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V), multiple fusion architectures (CNN-based, computation-based, attention-based), and detailed ablation studies covering calibration sensitivity, noise robustness, power consumption, and GPU memory scaling.
weaknesses: Modest novelty in individual algorithmic components: The underlying techniques (AdaRound, min-max calibration, KL/L2 feature distillation, and vector-quantized codebooks inspired by CodeFilling) are well-known primitives. The primary novelty lies in systems integration and domain-specific formulation rather than foundational quantization theory.

Hardware profiling mismatch: The latency and power profiling are primarily measured on a high-end desktop GPU (NVIDIA RTX 3090), which does not fully capture the memory hierarchy, compute characteristics, and integer arithmetic constraints of automotive-grade embedded edge SoCs (e.g., NVIDIA Drive Orin, Xavier, or low-power NPUs).

Ambiguity between PTQ and retraining: Section 2.3 states that codebook learning involves an unfreezing and joint training stage (optimizing detection loss and reconstruction loss over multiple epochs). This blurs the definition of an entirely training-free 'post-training quantization' pipeline, and the paper should clearer delineate the training compute/data cost incurred by the codebook learning stage versus the calibration stage.

Severe degradation on transformer-based architectures: As shown in Table 1, V2X-ViT suffers a massive drop under low precision (e.g., from 57.4/49.5 down to 29.9/8.8 at INT4/8), highlighting that the method does not yet adequately handle complex vision transformer architectures common in recent V2X perception works.

strengths: Practical and timely system-level focus: The paper addresses a critical deployment barrier in V2X cooperative perception by jointly optimizing model inference latency, GPU memory footprint, and transmission bandwidth.

Comprehensive full-stack design: Rather than treating quantization or communication compression in isolation, the authors integrate a multi-stage pipeline combining codebook-based message transmission with end-to-end post-training quantization (PTQ).

Domain-specific quantization adaptations: The proposed alignment losses (heterogeneity alignment via KL divergence and spatial alignment on predicted bounding boxes) effectively alleviate cross-agent feature distribution discrepancies and localization sensitivity under low bit-widths.

Rigorous evaluation on realistic and streaming benchmarks: The framework is evaluated across multiple datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V) and tested in online streaming environments (ROS-based V2X-ReaLO platform) with real hardware latency and power measurements via TensorRT on an RTX 3090.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty of core components is somewhat incremental: The codebook messaging largely draws upon existing vector/product quantization paradigms (e.g., CodeFilling [13]), and the PTQ optimization heavily builds on established techniques like AdaRound [28] and block-wise reconstruction [18], with domain adaptation via feature and output matching.

Inconsistency in precision settings between experimental sections: Section 3.1 primarily investigates aggressive INT4 weight / INT8 activation (INT4/8) quantization, whereas the system-level deployment experiments in Section 3.2 revert to INT8 weight / INT8 activation (INT8/8). A clearer justification for why INT4/8 was omitted from real-world TensorRT latency benchmarks should be provided in the main text.

Severe degradation on Transformer-based architectures: As shown in Table 1, V2X-ViT experiences severe degradation under quantization (AP50 drops from 49.5 to 11.0 in INT8/8 and 8.8 in INT4/8), highlighting a notable limitation of the proposed PTQ method when applied to attention mechanisms with layer normalization.

Mathematical typo in communication bandwidth expression: In Section 2.3, the communication volume is written as 'log2(H x W x C x 32 / 8)' and 'log2(H x W x log2(nL) x nR / 8)'. Prepending 'log2' to the total byte count is mathematically inaccurate when describing total transmitted volume/bandwidth.

strengths: Holistic and practical system perspective: Unlike most cooperative perception papers that assume ideal communication bandwidth and zero inference latency, this work tackles real-world deployment bottlenecks by unifying model quantization (PTQ) and communication compression (quantized codebook representations).

Domain-specific PTQ calibration designs: The paper introduces multi-agent sampling and fusion-stage alignment losses (heterogeneity alignment via KL divergence and spatial alignment on predicted bounding boxes) that specifically counteract cross-agent distribution shifts and spatial misalignment under low-bit precision.

Comprehensive experimental validation: The authors validate their method across multiple datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V), multiple fusion paradigms (CNN, computation-based, attention-based), and under both static offline metrics and dynamic real-world ROS/TensorRT streaming benchmarks (V2X-ReaLO).

Thorough analysis of system-level latency and scaling behavior: The decomposition of end-to-end latency into local compute, communication transmission, and fusion inference provides insightful evidence that latency reduction directly translates to improved perception accuracy in dynamic driving scenarios.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty of individual building blocks: The core components largely assemble established techniques—codebook compression builds closely upon CodeFilling [13], the PTQ framework relies on AdaRound [28] and standard MSE scale search, and the alignment objectives are conventional feature and prediction distillation losses.

Blurry boundary between PTQ and fine-tuning: While the quantization of network weights/activations is post-training, the codebook learning phase requires a two-stage training procedure that unfreezes and fine-tunes all model parameters using detection and reconstruction losses (Eq. 4). Presenting the framework strictly as lightweight PTQ partially obscures this required retraining overhead.

Severe degradation on transformer-based architectures: As shown in Table 1, attention-based models such as V2X-ViT experience catastrophic failure under INT4/INT8 (AP30 drops from 57.4 to 29.9, and AP50 drops to 8.8), indicating that the proposed alignment pipeline does not readily generalize to vision transformers without specialized quantization strategies.

Evaluation platform disparity: Latency and throughput benchmarks are reported on high-end desktop/workstation GPUs (NVIDIA RTX 3090 / A6000) rather than true automotive-grade edge SoCs (e.g., NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin or Drive Xavier), which would more accurately reflect practical in-vehicle deployment constraints.

Ambiguity in transmission protocol details: In Section 2.3, when multiple codes per location are used (nR > 1), it is unclear whether the combination weights alpha_r must also be quantized and transmitted alongside indices, or how much communication overhead they contribute.
